To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the MS/MS database searches may be reduced to pattern matching and that spectral networks analysis is a unique tool for identifying posttransitional modifications.

the MS/MS database searching can be reduced to extremely fast spectral pattern-matching and that the spectral networks analysis is an effective approach for identification of posttranslational modification sites.
spectral networks analysis can be used to (1) identify proteins, (2) identify modified peptides, and (3) identify posttranslational modification types.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for protein identification by MS/MS, which can be implemented in the existing MS/MS search engines.
the development of novel approaches for protein identification and characterization by MS/MS, which are based on a new concept of spectral networks analysis.
the development of a novel concept for protein identification by means of spectral network analysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed approach provides a novel paradigm that is capable of performing a MS/MS database query at a speed comparable to that of the existing database search tools.
the approach described herein allows one to identify a peptide by means of its MS/MS spectrum without ever comparing it against a database, thus greatly reducing the time of the identification.
our method allows one to identify peptides and to localize posttranslational and other modifications with high confidence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MS/MS database searching problem has been reduced from an extremely complex problem of comparing spectra against databases to a much simpler problem of matching spectra against patterns.
we are able to identify proteins and posttranslational modification sites in complex mixtures with a high degree of confidence and at a speed of 1 spectrum per second.
the MS/MS database searches are no longer necessary, as the MS/MS spectra are now being analyzed as a part of a network of spectra.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MS/MS database searches are not the bottleneck of MS/MS data processing and can be performed in a very efficient manner.
the spectral network approach can be used to perform MS/MS database searches, which is a significant step toward a more general framework for protein identification.
the existing approaches to protein identification can be improved by taking into consideration the fact that the MS/MS spectra from the same peptide are correlated.
